[PAPER_0039, relevance_score=0.319] As shown, varying amounts of preview would be expected on different fixations. But when the previews are averaged across these fixations, the resulting means (representing the amount of time spent processing words n + 1 and n + 2) would resemble gradients, with lexical processing being most efficient for the fixated word and being slower and less accurate for more distant words.

The Roles of Other Cognitive Variables During Lexical Processing

Because estimates of the perceptual span are derived from experiments in which participants read actual sentences, the estimates are probably inflated by the influence of higher-order factors on word identification.

[PAPER_0143, relevance_score=0.363] This prediction was confirmed.

In Experiments 2A and 2B, word naming was most rapid and accurate for stimuli that were displayed in central vision, with performance again decreasing monotonically with eccentricity for both measures. Comparing performance across experiments revealed that, although participants were more rapid and accurate naming words than making lexical decisions for centrally displayed stimuli, their overall performance was worse for word naming than lexical decisions, with the former task also being more adversely affected by eccentricity.

Arguably the most important of these variables was the impact of allowing versus restricting participants' eye movements.

[PAPER_0122, relevance_score=0.320] Results

Data Preparation and Analysis

The analysis approach for the naming accuracy and RT data was the same as in Experiments 1A and 1B. The models tested the fixed effect of stimulus position and controlled for log HAL target word frequency and word length. Preregistered analysis of untransformed RT and preregistered supplementary analyses examining interactions between stimulus position, word frequency, and length are provided in the online supplemental materials .

[PAPER_0125, relevance_score=0.396] [From Experiment 1B, cited for: Accuracy and response-time analysis approach] The fixed effect of stimulus position on lexical decision accuracy and response time (RT) was analyzed with (generalized) linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) using the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) in R (R Core Team, 2021).

[From Experiment 1B, cited for: Accuracy and response-time analysis approach] The RT data were log-transformed prior to analysis.

[PAPER_0127, relevance_score=0.388] [From Experiment 1B, cited for: Accuracy and response-time analysis approach] Models contained maximal random-effects structures, specifying intercepts and slopes for stimulus position across both participants and items (Barr et al., 2013).

For both experiments, the GLMM for accuracy included by-participant and by-item random intercepts and by-participant random slopes for stimulus position; the LMM for RT included by-participant and by-item random intercepts and random slopes for stimulus position but did not include the random correlation parameters. Models with more complex random-effects structures failed to converge.

[PAPER_0173, relevance_score=0.340] All of the simulations were completed using the actual words from our experiments and 1,000 statistical subjects per condition.

Simulation 1 began with the simplest starting assumptions: that lexical decisions are unbiased (i.e., pG = .5) and naming requires completely accurate word identification (i.e., pG = 0). The values of the parameters DMT and θR were found for each experiment via grid searches of the parameter space (see Footnote 3) using the RMSD between the observed and simulated condition means as the goodness-of-fit metric.
